1.note: קַו הַשָּׁוֶה, "the equal line", is the usual medieval Hebrew term for the equator. Here it seems to mean one line running from Babylon in the east to Spain in the west. The geography is the author's; the rendering is uncertain.

2.note: "Joined and parted" (מְחֻבָּר וּמְפֹרָד) may describe the art of poetry (composing and analysing, or verse that is joined and divided into halves) or the sages (united and scattered). Uncertain.

3.he: וַיְהִי בִשְׁנַת אַרְבַּעַת אֲלָפִים וּשְׁבַע מֵאוֹת לַיְצִירָה
3.note: Year 4700 of the Creation is 939/940 CE. The "seventh century" is the 700s of the fifth millennium (940–1040 CE); the "eighth" and "ninth" below follow from it. The chronology is the author's.

4.note: עַל הַשְּׁמִינִית, "upon the Sheminith" ("the eighth"), is a musical term in the headings of Ps 6 and 12. It is a pun on "the eighth century" in the line before.

5.note: The patron meant is Ḥasdai ibn Shaprut (about 915–975), the son of Isaac. The text gives the names the other way round: "Isaac son of Ḥasdai".

6.note: A pun on מַדָּע (learning) and מוֹדַע (kinsman), with Boaz, the kinsman (Ruth 2:1) and redeemer (Ruth 2:20).

7.note: Solomon ibn Gabirol, who called himself "the small" (הַקָּטָן) in his poems.

8.note: תּוֹר is "turtledove" (Song 2:12, after "the blossoms" two lines before) and also "row, order". A play on תּוֹר / תּוֹרָה.

9.note: The four are a kingdom of poetry: Solomon ibn Gabirol the king, Abraham ibn Ezra his Nasi, Judah Halevi his captain, Moses ibn Ezra his prophet. The names fit the biblical roles (Solomon, Abraham, Judah, Moses).

10.note: A play on נִיגַע (we toil) and נִגַּע (we touch).

11.note: Dishon and Alvan are descendants of Seir the Horite (Gen 36:21, 23), not places. They seem to be chosen for the rhyme with יָוָן (Greece); the sense of the phrase is uncertain.

12.note: The source has וְעַל; Project Ben-Yehuda's footnote (the last line of the gate) says to read וְאַל, "and not". Translated so.

13.note: A pun: קֳדָשִׁים, "holy things", and קְדֵשִׁים, "cult prostitutes" (Deut 23:18).

14.note: הֲתֻלִּים is read from התל, "to mock, deceive" (Job 13:9; 1 Kgs 18:27): the false parts of the poem. Uncertain.

15.note: The Almohad ruler of North Africa and al-Andalus. "The time of the persecution" (הַשְּׁמַד) in the next lines is the Almohad persecution of the Jews from the 1140s.

16.he: רַבִּי יוֹסֵף בַּר יְהוּדָה בַּר שִׁמְעוֹן
16.note: Probably Joseph ben Judah ibn Shimʿon, from the Maghreb, the pupil of Maimonides, who settled in Aleppo. The maqama "Thus says Tobiah ben Zedekiah" is attributed to him.

17.note: No-amon (Nah 3:8) is Alexandria in medieval Hebrew.

18.note: A play on רֹאשׁ: "chief" spices (בְּשָׂמִים רֹאשׁ, Exod 30:23) and רוֹשׁ, "gall, poison" (Deut 29:17).

19.note: Each poet is put down with a pun on his biblical namesake: Solomon "the Small" (ibn Gabirol) too small; Abram "very heavy" (Gen 13:2, with cattle; here Abraham ibn Ezra); Moses (ibn Ezra) a mere shepherd (Exod 3:1); Judah (Halevi) shall "acknowledge" him (Gen 49:8 יְהוּדָה ... יוֹדוּךָ).

20.he: שְׂחוֹק עָשָׂה לִי אֱלֹהִים וְכָל הַשּׁוֹמֵעַ לִי יִצְחָק
20.note: Gen 21:6, Sarah at the birth of Isaac (יִצְחָק): a pun on the poet's name, Isaac. In Genesis "laugh" is joyful; here it is mockery.

21.note: Zobah is Aleppo in medieval Hebrew.

22.note: A pun on the name Ṣemaḥ: צֶמַח, "a stalk", of Hos 8:7, "the stalk yields no meal".

23.note: Probably Judah ibn ʿAbbas, a poet of the 12th century who lived in Fez and later in Aleppo.

24.note: Calneh (Gen 10:10) is identified with al-Raqqa on the Euphrates.

25.note: Literally "of the masters of the first watch": perhaps the first rank (or the first course of priests, 1 Chr 24:7). Ironic. Uncertain.

26.note: m. Beitzah 5:3: an animal and utensils may go on the Sabbath only as far as their owner may. Here: the community is no better than its poet.

27.note: The poem opens with "Curses", against the poet's name, Berakhot, "Blessings".

28.he: יְצִיאוֹת הָעֲנָק אֲשֶׁר לְרַבִּי משֶׁה בֶּן עֶזְרָא
28.note: The ʿAnaq ("Necklace", also called Tarshish) is Moses ibn Ezra's book of short poems on homonyms. יְצִיאוֹת, "exits", is read as the closing lines or rhyme words of its poems. Uncertain.

29.note: Ben ha-Sekhvi means "son of the cock"; hence the jibe from Job 38:36, "who gave understanding to the cock" (שֶׂכְוִי).

30.note: יִרְכְּכֶנָּה, "will soften her", is read as "will enjoy her", with Deut 28:30 in the next line. A reading יִרְכָּבֶנָּה, "will ride her", is also possible. Uncertain.

31.note: Aden in Yemen, written as עֲדִינָה, "the pleasure-loving one" of Isa 47:8.

32.note: A rhyme of לְשׁוֹנִי (my tongue) and קִלְּשׁוֹנִי (my trident or fork, 1 Sam 13:21). Ḥever's name also puns on חָבֵר, "companion", in the line before.
